reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
setup: Historical simulation on 100 daily returns. The ten worst, in %: $-3.2, -2.6, -2.4, -2.0, -1.9, -1.7, -1.5, -1.5, -1.2, -0.7$. The VaR is the $(\alpha n + 1)$th worst observation. Returns are i.i.d. and a month has 20 trading days.
ask: The 95% one-month VaR is closest to:

options.why: Divided the daily VaR by $\sqrt{20}$ instead of multiplying: $1.70 / 4.47 = 0.38\%$. Time scaling makes the longer-horizon VaR bigger.
Stopped at the daily VaR and never scaled it to a month.
Multiplied by 20 days instead of $\sqrt{20}$: $1.70 \times 20 = 34\%$. Independent daily returns add in variance, not in a straight line.

takeaway: Rank first (the $(\alpha n+1)$th worst is the cut-off), then scale by $\sqrt{\text{days}}$, not by the number of days.

reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
setup: Historical simulation on 100 monthly returns. The ten worst, in %: $-12, -7, -32, -26, -24, -20, -19, -17, -15, -14$. The VaR is the $(\alpha n + 1)$th worst observation. The data are already monthly.
ask: The 95% monthly VaR (as a loss) is:

options.why: Took the 5th worst ($\alpha n = 5$) and dropped the $+1$ in $(\alpha n + 1)$.
Averaged the 5th and 6th worst. The convention here picks a single observation, the 6th.
Used the single worst return, which is the 100% (maximum loss) end, not the 95% quantile.

takeaway: Count ranks from the worst loss: 5% of 100 observations is 5, and the convention reads the next one, the 6th.

reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
setup: Annually compounded spot rates: 1-year 4%, 2-year 9%. A 1-year investment today followed by a 1-year investment at the forward rate $f$ must match the 2-year spot investment, $(1+s_2)^2 = (1+s_1)(1+f)$.
ask: The forward rate for the year starting one year from now is:

options.label: Between 4% and 9%
options.why: Took the simple difference $9\% - 4\% = 5\%$ (or an average). The two years of 9% must be earned in total, so a weak first year forces a much stronger second.

options.label: Below 4%
options.why: Inverted the ratio: $1.04^2/1.09 - 1 = -0.8\%$. The 2-year growth factor goes in the numerator.

takeaway: A forward rate is the rate that closes the gap between two spot rates, so with a low 1-year rate it lands above the 2-year spot (roughly $2s_2 - s_1$).

reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
setup: Pure expectations with certainty. The one-year rate is 11.316% today and will be 13.457% next year and 15.658% the year after (annual compounding). The 2-year spot rate has already been found: 12.38%.
ask: The 3-year spot rate is closest to:

options.why: Stopped at the 2-year spot rate; the third year's rate was never brought in.
Took the last one-year rate as the 3-year spot. A spot rate averages all three years.
Reported the total three-year growth $1.46071 - 1$ and never took the cube root.

takeaway: Spot rate = geometric average of the one-year rates, so it sits between the lowest and highest rate and below their total growth.

reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
setup: All investors expect the one-year rate to be 6% now, 8% next year and 10% the year after. The 3-year spot rate is the annualised rate over those three years (annual compounding). The simple average of the three rates is 8.00%.
ask: Compared with 8.00%, the 3-year spot rate is:

options.label: Above 8.00%
options.why: Reasoned that compounding makes the total growth exceed $3 \times 8\%$ (25.93% against 24%). Annualising takes a cube root, and a geometric mean never exceeds the arithmetic mean.

options.label: Exactly 8.00%
options.why: Used the simple average of the rates. The gap is small (about 1.2 bp) but the geometric mean is strictly lower when the rates differ.

takeaway: The geometric mean of the one-year rates is always a touch below their arithmetic mean; the more dispersed the rates, the bigger the gap.

reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
setup: Risk-neutral investors, no risk premium. The one-year rate is 8% today and will be 11% or 5% in a year, each with probability 50% (expected rate 8%). A two-year zero pays USD 1,000.
ask: The tree price of the two-year zero, against USD 1,000/1.08$^2$ = USD 857.34 (priced at the expected rate), is:

options.label: Lower
options.why: Treated rate uncertainty as a cost. Bond prices are convex in rates, so the up-move loses less than the down-move gains.

options.label: The same
options.why: Assumed the expected rate gives the expected price. That holds only if price were linear in the rate.

takeaway: Jensen's inequality: $E[1/(1+r)] > 1/(1+E[r])$, so a risk-neutral tree prices above the flat-rate price.

reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
setup: Risk-neutral tree, 50% on every branch. One-year rate: 8% today; 10% or 6% in one year; 12%, 8% or 4% in two years. The value of convexity (8% less the implied spot rate) is 1.85 bp for the two-year zero.
ask: For the three-year zero it is closest to:

options.label: ≈ 15 bp
options.why: Used the cumulative three-year gap ($3 \times 4.9$ bp) instead of the annualised spot-rate gap.

options.label: ≈ 0.5 bp
options.why: Scale slip (one tenth): the gap is in basis points, $0.0494\%$ is 4.9 bp, not 0.49.

options.label: ≈ 1.9 bp
options.why: Carried the two-year figure over. The effect grows with maturity because more convex pieces are added.

takeaway: The value of convexity grows faster than maturity: 1.85 bp at two years, about 4.9 bp at three.

reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
setup: The one-year rate is 8.0%. Risk-averse investors require 50 bp per year of duration risk, counted on the bond as it will stand at the end of the holding period. You buy a three-year zero and hold it for one year, when it becomes a two-year zero.
ask: The risk premium earned over the year is:

options.why: Counted one year, the length of the holding period, rather than the bond's duration at the end of it.
Used the three-year duration the bond has today; the premium is for the two-year bond it becomes.

takeaway: The premium is $\lambda \times$ (duration at the end of the holding period), not at the start.

reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
setup: The short rate is 3.0%, the risk premium is 15 bp per unit of duration, and a bond has duration 6 and convexity 50. Rate volatility is 1.5% a year, so a convexity term $\tfrac12 C\sigma^2$ is about 0.56%. The risk-averse investor's expected return is $r_0 + \lambda D = 3.90\%$ before any convexity adjustment.
ask: The expected one-year return, compared with 3.90%, is:

options.label: Higher, about 4.46%
options.why: Added the convexity gain $0.56\%$ to the return. In expected return it is offset by the lower forward rates it implies, so nothing is added.

options.label: Lower, about 3.34%
options.why: Subtracted the convexity term. Convexity enters the forward rate with a minus sign, not the expected return.

takeaway: Expected return = $r_0 + \lambda D$. Convexity lowers the forward rate but does not change the expected return.

setup: Basel backtesting of a 99% one-day VaR: 8 exceptions in 250 days. Causes: 4 volatile markets and changed correlations; 2 too few maturity buckets in the model; 1 intraday trading changed positions; 1 major earthquake. The supervisor excludes only what the rules allow.
ask: How many exceptions count towards the multiplier $k$?

options.why: Counted all exceptions. A natural disaster is an allowed exclusion.
Counted only the bad-luck exceptions; model-accuracy and intraday ones are penalised too.
Counted only the model-fault and intraday exceptions; market-volatility exceptions are expected some of the time but still count.

takeaway: Only abnormal events (a disaster, a political shock) may be excluded; volatility, model flaws and intraday trading all count.

setup: A USD 200m portfolio of a 2-year and a 4-year 5% par bond (USD 100m each). Average principal maturity is 3.00 years; Macaulay duration is 2.84 years. Monthly 95% VaR of zeros: 2y 0.9868%, 3y 1.4841%. VaR is mapped to the duration, with linear interpolation.
ask: The duration-mapped VaR, against the principal-mapped VaR (the 3-year vertex), is:

options.label: Higher
options.why: Used the 3.00-year principal maturity, or read a longer horizon into the portfolio. The duration is shorter at 2.84 years.

options.label: The same
options.why: Treated both maturity measures as one. Duration is below average principal maturity because coupons arrive early.

takeaway: Coupons pull duration below average maturity of principal, so duration mapping gives a slightly lower VaR.

reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
setup: A corporate yield (daily change standard deviation 4.20 bp) is regressed on a Treasury yield (4.40 bp). The regression has a positive slope and $R^2 = 77.5\%$, so the correlation is about 0.88.
ask: The hedge adjustment factor $\beta$, compared with the correlation, is:

options.label: Larger
options.why: Flipped the volatility ratio: $0.88 \times 4.40/4.20 = 0.92$. Beta puts the hedged yield's volatility on top.

options.label: Equal
options.why: Treated $R^2$ or the correlation as the slope. $\beta = \rho\,\sigma_{corp}/\sigma_{Tsy}$ equals $\rho$ only if the volatilities match.

takeaway: $\beta = \rho\,\sigma_y/\sigma_x$: it is the correlation scaled by the ratio of volatilities, so it is below $\rho$ when the hedged yield is the calmer one.

reading: MR-11: Regression Hedging and Principal Component Analysis
setup: A trader holds CAD 50m face of a 30-year provincial bond and sells the Government of Canada 30-year bond as a hedge. DV01 per 100 face: provincial 0.1835, GoC 0.2010. The regression of provincial yield changes on GoC yield changes has slope $\beta = 0.91$.
ask: The face amount of the GoC bond to sell, against CAD 50m, is:

options.label: More than CAD 50m
options.why: Inverted the DV01 ratio ($50 \times 0.2010/0.1835 = 54.8$). The GoC bond has the larger DV01 per face, so less face is needed.

options.label: About CAD 50m
options.why: Matched face for face and ignored both the DV01 ratio and the regression slope.

takeaway: Hedge face $= F \times \text{DV01 ratio} \times \beta$. With both factors below 1, the hedge is smaller than the position.

reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
setup: A tree moves the six-month rate (2.00% today) up or down by 50 bp each step. The true up probability is 0.50. Calibrating to the zero prices gives a risk-neutral up probability of 0.8009 for the first step.
ask: Under the risk-neutral process, the expected six-month rate at the next date (6 months out) is:

options.why: Used the true probabilities: symmetric moves leave no drift. The risk-neutral up probability is 0.8009.
Counted only the up-moves: $0.8009 \times 50 = 40$ bp. The down-moves (probability 0.1991) subtract.
Assumed the rate always moves up by the full 50 bp.

takeaway: Drift per step is $(2p - 1)$ times the step size: risk-neutral $p$ above 0.5 pushes the expected rate up.

reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
setup: A semiannual tree has a six-month rate of 4.00% (a bond at the short rate would earn 2.00% over six months). A security trades at an option-adjusted spread of $-20$ bp. The OAS is expected to stay constant, and the process is risk-neutral.
ask: The security's expected return over the next six months, against 2.00%, is:

options.label: Above 2.00%
options.why: Added the OAS with the wrong sign: $(4.00 + 0.20)/2 = 2.10\%$. A negative OAS means the security is rich and earns less.

options.label: Equal to 2.00%
options.why: Applied the risk-neutral rule that expected return equals the short rate, forgetting that the OAS is added to the rate.

takeaway: Expected return $= (r_0 + \text{OAS})\,dt$: a negative OAS (rich security) earns less than the short rate.

reading: MR-12: Arbitrage Pricing with Term Structure Models
setup: A one-year CMT swap pays the receiver $\text{USD } 2\text{m} \times (y - 4.00\%)/2$ every six months. The six-month rate is 4.00% today and moves $\pm 40$ bp per step. The risk-neutral up probabilities are 0.65 (first step) and 0.58 (second); the desk's true probability is 0.50.
ask: The swap's value to the receiver is:

options.label: Zero
options.why: Reasoned that a swap struck at today's rate starts at zero. The risk-neutral up-moves (0.65, 0.58) make expected payments positive.

options.label: Negative
options.why: Used the true 0.50 probabilities and let discounting dominate: that gives about $-\$8$. Pricing must use the risk-neutral probabilities.

takeaway: Pricing uses risk-neutral probabilities: a risk-neutral up-drift makes a swap receiving the rate worth more than zero.

reading: MR-13: Expectations, Risk Premium, Convexity, and the Shape of the Term Structure
setup: A forward rate is built from the short rate of 2.5% plus three terms for a zero with duration 7: expectations ($D \times$ the 0.3% expected annual change in the short rate), risk premium ($15$ bp per year of duration) and a convexity effect of 0.65% that is subtracted.
ask: The net amount added to the 2.5% short rate is:

options.label: +3.80 pp
options.why: Added the convexity effect instead of subtracting it.

options.label: +3.15 pp
options.why: Left the convexity effect out altogether.

options.label: $-0.20$ pp
options.why: Forgot to multiply by duration: $0.30 + 0.15 - 0.65 = -0.20$. Expectations and premium scale with $D$.

takeaway: Expectations and premium scale with duration; convexity comes off the forward rate even though it adds to bond returns.
